content: Intimate partner violence (IPV) against women is a widespread issue and is closely linked to mental health problems. Women who experience IPV often seek healthcare services for mental health concerns. The World Health Organization recommends evidence-based mental health treatments for women who have experienced IPV and have a mental health diagnosis. However, it remains unclear whether psychological therapies are effective for these women and whether they might cause harm. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of psychological therapies for women who experience IPV. The primary outcomes assessed were depression, self-efficacy, and harm (measured by dropout rates) at six to 12 months of follow-up. Secondary outcomes included other mental health symptoms, anxiety, quality of life, re-exposure to IPV, safety planning and behaviors, use of healthcare and IPV services, and social support. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, cluster-RCTs, and cross-over trials involving women aged 16 years or older who self-reported recent or lifetime IPV. Trials were included if participants also had co-existing mental health diagnoses or substance abuse issues. Psychological therapies encompassed a variety of interventions targeting cognition, motivation, and behavior, and were compared to usual care, no treatment, or minimal interventions. The therapies were categorized based on the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders psychological therapies list. Data from 33 trials involving 5,517 women were analyzed. Of these, 2,798 women (51%) were assigned to psychological therapy interventions, while 2,719 women (49%) were in comparator groups. The therapies included integrative therapies (11 trials), humanistic therapies (9 trials), cognitive behavioral therapy (6 trials), third-wave cognitive behavioral therapies (4 trials), and other psychologically-oriented interventions (3 trials). No trials involved psychodynamic therapies. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, with the majority in the United States. Participants were recruited from healthcare, community, shelter, or refuge settings, and the therapies were primarily delivered face-to-face. The number of therapy sessions ranged from 2 to 50, and the providers included social workers, nurses, psychologists, community health workers, family doctors, and researchers. The average age of participants was 37 years, and 66% were unemployed. Approximately half of the women were married or living with a partner. Just over half of the participants had experienced IPV in the past 12 months, 6% in the past two years, and 42% during their lifetime. While 61% of the trials used reliable random-sampling strategies, only 36% adequately concealed participant allocation. Nineteen trials measured depression, but only four assessed it as a continuous outcome at medium-term follow-up. These four trials, involving 600 women, showed that psychological therapies probably reduce depression (SMD −0.24, 95% CI −0.47 to −0.01; moderate-certainty evidence). However, for self-efficacy, there was no evidence of a difference between groups (SMD −0.12, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.09; one trial, 346 women; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in dropout rates between experimental and comparator groups, suggesting no harm (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.44; five trials, 840 women; low-certainty evidence). No trials reported adverse events related to psychological therapies, and only one trial used a validated scale to measure harm. For secondary outcomes, anxiety was assessed only at short-term follow-up, with evidence suggesting that psychological therapies may reduce anxiety symptoms (SMD −0.96, 95% CI −1.29 to −0.63; four trials, 158 women; low-certainty evidence). At medium-term follow-up, there was no evidence of differences between groups for safety planning (SMD 0.04, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.25; one trial, 337 women), post-traumatic stress disorder (SMD −0.24, 95% CI −0.54 to 0.06; four trials, 484 women), or re-exposure to IPV (SMD 0.03, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.2; two trials, 547 women). In conclusion, psychological therapies likely reduce depression and may reduce anxiety in women who experience IPV. However, there is uncertainty regarding their impact on other outcomes, such as self-efficacy, post-traumatic stress disorder, re-exposure to IPV, and safety planning. Additionally, data on harm are limited. While psychological therapies may improve emotional health, it is unclear whether they address women's broader needs for safety, support, and recovery from complex trauma. Further research is needed, particularly interventions focused on trauma-informed approaches and more rigorous trials with consistent outcome measures and follow-up time points.
